title: Sequence Length Scaling and Kernel Breakpoints — characterization and operational playbook
author: Anika Rao
content:
Overview

This page documents an empirical characterization of how sequence length distribution interacts with kernel selection and scheduling in the Redwood serving runtime. It consolidates the benchmark design, observed kernel breakpoints, profiling steps, and an operational runbook for diagnosing and mitigating performance cliffs that appear when request token lengths cross specific thresholds. The goal is to provide a reproducible approach for teams to:

- quantify per-model breakpoints where the runtime swaps execution kernels or changes memory strategy,
- map those breakpoints to tail and p50 latency regressions under realistic traffic mixes, and
- provide a low-friction remediation path (config, routing, and rollout guidance).

Why this matters

Sequence length interacts with many runtime subsystems: attention kernel selection, KV-cache allocation, beam/decoder loop scheduling, and cross-GPU shard placement. Small shifts in length distribution (e.g., 64 -> 96 tokens) can cause:

- kernel fallback to slower attention implementations,
- increased temporary GPU memory pressure that triggers spilling or allocator pathologies,
- larger per-request batching mismatches that break latency SLOs, and
- degraded model quantization code-paths (fp16->int8 fallback) on older kernels.

This doc summarizes controlled experiments and provides playbooks to identify and mitigate these effects in production.

Principles and definitions

1) Breakpoint: a sequence length value at which the runtime changes kernel, memory allocation pattern, or scheduling policy.
2) Hot path kernel: the primary highly-optimized kernel chosen for the majority of requests below the first breakpoint.
3) Slow path kernel: fallback kernel or non-optimized path taken above a breakpoint.
4) Effective length: request length + expected generated tokens when the runtime preallocates KV or scratch.

Experiment summary (high level)

- Workload: 10k synthetic prompts per model, sampled across prompt templates used by product teams (short chat, multi-turn context, doc summary). Generation budgets: 16, 64, 128 tokens.
- Models: two LLaMA-family variants (7B, 13B), a non-sharded 70B, and a trimmed 3B quantized.
- Hardware: A100-40GB (single-GPU runs), A100-80GB (single and 2-way sharded), H100-80GB (single-GPU), and RTX-6000 for legacy stack tests.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel name (telemetry tag), GPU mem high-water, scheduler queue depth, batch composition, and KV-cache hit/miss rate.

Key observed breakpoints (example)

| Model | Observed breakpoints (tokens) | Typical effect | Notes |
|-------|-------------------------------:|----------------|-------|
| 3B-quant | 96, 256 | 96 triggers slower attention kernel (vectorized->scalar), 256 triggers allocator spilling | quantization path causes extra memory copies on GPU_Legacy drivers |
| 7B-sharded | 64, 192 | 64->192 increases per-shard KV footprint; above 192 scheduler switches to larger slice size causing +40% p95 | shard placement tuning recommended |
| 13B | 80 | kernel switch to tiled attention; p99 spikes for small batch sizes | tiling increases kernel launch overhead |
| 70B | 64, 128 | 64 increases async memcpy contention; 128 often requires 2-shard execution which changes network RTTs | check NCCL tuning |

Benchmark methodology (repro steps)

1) Environment setup
   - Use the perf harness in tools/runtime-bench. Ensure CUDA visible devices set and driver/harness versions recorded.
   - Commands (example):

     ```bash
     export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
     git checkout main && bazel build //tools/runtime-bench:bench_runner
     ./bazel-bin/tools/runtime-bench/bench_runner \\n       --model-path gs://redwood-models/llama-7b --run-config configs/bench/seqscale-2026.yaml \
       --target-rt a100-40gb --iterations 10000 --seed 42
     ```

2) Sequence sweep
   - Sweep effective lengths: [8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 128, 160, 192, 256] with fixed gen budget where applicable.
   - For each length record: kernel_name, batch_size, queue_wait_ms, gpu_mem_mb, p50/p95/p99 latency.

3) Mixed traffic test
   - Construct realistic traffic mix from product telemetry (ratios e.g., 70% short-chat (<=64), 20% medium (65-160), 10% long).
   - Run under target concurrency and measure tail latencies and KV cache hit rate.

4) Repeat across hardware and driver versions to separate hardware/compiler effects.

Telemetry tags to capture

- kernel.name
- kernel.variant
- scheduler.queue_depth
- batch.composition
- kvcache.size
- alloc.high_water_mb
- api.request_effective_length
- model.shard_count

Analysis guide

- Identify the first length where kernel.name changes for >1% of requests; call that L1.
- Plot p95/p99 by length and overlay kernel.name. Breakpoints appear where latency changes sharply with correlated kernel switch.
- Correlate alloc.high_water_mb with p99 spikes: if mem rises by >10% at a breakpoint, consider quantization/alloc path investigation.

Operational playbook (triage + remediation)

1) Detect
   - Alerting: create an alert when model.route p99 latency increases by >25% vs 7d baseline and kernel.name for >5% of requests is a known slow path. Use telemetry query:

     ```sql
     SELECT kernel_name, count(*) FROM runtime.events
     WHERE model_name = 'llama-7b' AND ts > now() - interval '5m'
     GROUP BY kernel_name ORDER BY count DESC
     ```

2) Triage steps (ordered)
   - Confirm whether p99 increase maps to shift in request length distribution (compare api.request_effective_length histograms).
   - Check scheduler.queue_depth and batch.composition to rule out batch skew.
   - Verify KV-cache hit rate; a sudden drop can inflate effective length due to upstream re-fetching.
   - Inspect GPU alloc.high_water_mb for leaking/spill behavior.

3) Immediate mitigation (fast path)
   - If kernel switch caused regression and a faster compatible kernel exists for longer lengths, enable temporary model override to force that kernel for this model/route (use route-level config). Example: set runtime.override_kernel = "attention-tiled-opt-v2" for routes matching /chat/* .
   - If KV-cache is the issue, enable short-term per-route prefix-caching or reduce prefix size to avoid crossing the breakpoint.

4) Medium-term remediations
   - Add a routing rule: split traffic by predicted effective length (<=L1 vs >L1) and route long requests to a node pool with larger GPUs or a kernel-optimized pool.
   - Adjust autoscaler warm targets for nodes that serve long sequences to avoid cold-shard placement during bursts.
   - Work with runtime team to prioritize kernel optimization (see section below).

5) Postmortem items
   - Add failing prompt examples to the model’s regression set and schedule quantized-kernel compatibility test in nightly perf suite.
   - Update per-model sequence breakpoints table in team wiki and annotate deployment manifests with expected L1/L2.

Kernel scheduling and compilation action items

- For each runtime kernel variant, maintain a short compatibility matrix: supported sequence ranges, preferred hardware, and quantization compatibility.
- Where a kernel has a small but expensive launch overhead (tiling kernels), include a warm-start micro-benchmark in the perf suite to measure amortized cost vs per-request overhead.
- Add compiler flag matrix to CI for kernels that use vendor-provided fused ops — this prevents unexpected fallbacks when new drivers are rolled.

Profiler playbook (how to collect actionable traces)

1) Light-weight trace (2–5 mins under live traffic)
   - Capture telemetry tags listed above at 5s granularity.
   - Export top-3 kernel_name occurrences with latency percentiles.

2) Full GPU profile (for repro)
   - Use NVIDIA Nsight Systems and measure kernel launches, memcpy, and occupancy. Command example:

     ```bash
     nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn --sample=timer --output seq-breakpoint-7b \\n       -- ./bazel-bin/tools/runtime-bench/bench_runner --model llama-7b --length 96 --iterations 1000
     ```

3) Kernel-level microprofile
   - Capture kernel-level flamegraphs and symbolized traces. Correlate with allocator calls to find allocation hotspots that precede kernel fallback.

Configuration table (suggested thresholds and overrides)

| Config key | Recommended default | When to change | Owner |
|------------|---------------------|----------------|-------|
| runtime.seq_breakpoint_override[model] | unset | When production L1 causes SLO breach and fast kernel is known | runtime-kernel-team |
| runtime.route_length_routing.enabled | true | For routes with >10% long requests | infra-ops |
| runtime.kvcache.max_prefix_tokens | 256 | Reduce if crossing L1 frequently | modeling |
| autoscaler.warm_target_long_seq | 2 nodes | Increase when long requests cause shard cold starts | srescaling |

Notes on experiments that produced these values

- All experiments were run with GPU driver 535.xx and CUDA 11.8 unless noted. On H100 with CUDA 12.x some breakpoints shifted by ±8 tokens due to different kernel tiling defaults.
- Quantized models showed more frequent kernel fallbacks on legacy drivers; driver upgrades removed one observed breakpoint in the 3B-quant tests.

Runbook snippets (quick commands)

- Force route-level kernel override:

  ```bash
  redwoodctl routes update --route /chat/llama-7b --set runtime.override_kernel=attention-tiled-opt-v2
  ```

- Add temporary length split rule (route annotations):

  ```yaml
  routes:
    - name: chat-short
      match: /chat/*
      predicate: "api.request_effective_length <= 64"
      pool: short-seq-pool
    - name: chat-long
      match: /chat/*
      predicate: "api.request_effective_length > 64"
      pool: long-seq-pool
  ```

Knowledge transfer and next steps

- Owners: runtime-kernel-team (kernel optimization and flags), infra-ops (routing and pools), modeling (prefix sizing guidance).
- Add a nightly test to the benchmarking suite: seqscale-nightly that runs the sequence sweep for all production models and records L1/L2 breakpoints to a central table.
- Track kernel regressions as part of release gating for runtime releases; a change that introduces a new breakpoint must have a documented mitigation and perf test.

Appendix A — reproducible artifacts and results

- Benchmark configs: gs://redwood-perf/seqscale-2026/{llama-3b,7b,13b,70b}.yaml
- Raw telemetry snapshot (airgapped): s3://redwood-archives/perf/seqscale-2026/summary.tar.gz
- Notebooks: internal link to notebooks showing plotting routines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/seqscale-visualizations

Appendix B — known caveats

- Breakpoints are sensitive to driver and compiler versions; do not copy absolute token values between clusters without running the sweep.
- Mixed-batch workloads can mask breakpoints due to amortized kernel launch costs; both isolated and mixed tests are required.
- Some models employ decoding-time length conditioning that changes effective length distribution; ensure input generation in benchmarks replicates production preprocessors.

If you have questions, want the raw experiment logs, or need help adding a model to the nightly sweep, ping the runtime-kernel-team in #runtime-kernel and assign a short task in the infra-ops backlog.
